endorsements.quote: Moreover, as for every new treatment concepts, AI-based approaches need to demonstrate their superiority in well-designed clinical trials.

There is no perfect technical solution against such biases, but it is critical that both scientists and developers who set up the machine learning / AI system, as well as the end users, are made aware of them.
It is, therefore, imperative that the ability to assess the outputs of such artificial intelligence systems is part of medical education and training.

unlisted_practices: Include anonymized raw data from the start of AI training where possible.
Obtain ethical approval and patient informed consent before using and evaluating patient-related data for AI.
Treat AI computed results as additional evidence that helps clinicians gain a more complete picture, integrating AI into clinical reasoning carefully.
Medical professional societies should set up and implement further-training curricula on AI for doctors.
Develop new clinical trial concepts, including new randomized controlled trial designs, to evaluate AI efficacy.
Develop additional strategies for explainability to enable informed clinical decisions.
Build the medical informatics infrastructure needed to accompany the transition to AI-assisted care.
Clinicians should work with patients and patient advocacy groups to ensure AI does not disadvantage patient groups by ethnicity, age or other characteristics.
Require rigorous clinical evidence before AI image analysis systems are used broadly in clinical routine.

screen.reason: This is an expert consensus statement and roadmap/framework paper regarding artificial intelligence deployment and applications in hematology and oncology.
